ideas.hypothesis: New rail station areas that adopt inclusive planning tools (affordable housing set-asides, land banking) before station opening will show lower outflow of low-income renters over five years than comparable station areas without such tools.

sources.role: mechanism/measure: transit-rich neighborhoods price out renters; equitable policy tools
finding: case studies of revitalization without displacement
setting: St. Louis Delmar Loop TOD inclusion assessment

ideas.test: Compare census tracts within 0.5 mile of 20-40 new US rail stations, coded for pre-opening inclusionary policies, using ACS/census data on low-income renter share change versus matched control tracts (difference-in-differences).
ideas.disconfirming: Low-income renter loss is equal or greater in station areas with inclusive tools.

ideas.hypothesis: TOD-driven displacement of low-income transit users increases metropolitan income segregation by relocating displaced households to lower-transit-access tracts, raising dissimilarity indices along new transit corridors.

sources.role: mechanism: core transit users replaced by car-owning higher-income residents
setting/measure: socio-spatial implications of TOD
finding: counter-cases with revitalization without displacement

ideas.test: Using decennial census/ACS tract data for metros that opened light rail 2000-2010, compute income dissimilarity indices before and after and compare corridor vs non-corridor changes; trace moves with longitudinal address data if available.
ideas.disconfirming: Segregation indices do not rise, or fall, along new transit corridors relative to controls.

ideas.hypothesis: TOD station areas with context-sensitive thoroughfare design (narrower lanes, frequent crossings) generate higher walk mode share than TOD areas of similar density with conventional arterials.

sources.role: mechanism/method: ITE context-sensitive thoroughfare design for walkability
mechanism: New Urbanism compact walkable neighborhoods for greener travel
setting/method: identifying TOD areas in Vancouver

ideas.test: Audit street design at 30 Vancouver SkyTrain station areas and link to regional travel survey walk mode shares, controlling for density and income.
ideas.disconfirming: Thoroughfare design has no significant association with walk share after controlling for density.

ideas.hypothesis: Zoning that permits mixed uses increases neighborhood land-use diversity scores, which in turn reduce household vehicle hours traveled, with the zoning effect operating mainly through diversity rather than density.

sources.role: measure: elasticities of travel demand to diversity
mechanism: land-use policy affects VMT/VHT
measure: transit readiness scorecard for diversity
mechanism: land use and active transport

ideas.test: In one metro, code parcel zoning (mixed-use permitted share) by block group, compute entropy diversity, link to household travel survey VHT, and run mediation analysis.
ideas.disconfirming: Mixed-use zoning does not raise diversity, or diversity has no effect on VHT.

ideas.hypothesis: Infill development with reduced parking requirements produces lower auto mode share among new residents than infill with standard parking, indicating parking policy moderates the urban form-travel link.

sources.role: finding/setting: Berkeley parking management and TOD mode shares
mechanism: financing constraints of infill/TOD
finding: travel in traditional urban forms
mechanism: causality debate between urban form and mobility

ideas.test: Survey residents of 10-20 recent infill buildings in one city, varying in parking ratios, on mode choice and car ownership, controlling for self-selection attitudes.
ideas.disconfirming: Auto mode share is unrelated to parking ratio after controlling for attitudes.

ideas.hypothesis: Zones with transit-oriented design features exhibit lower auto trip rates and this effect is larger in rapidly sprawling outer zones than in core zones of a metropolitan region.

sources.role: method/finding: SUR models of zone-based travel in Seoul
mechanism: regional growth management versus sprawl
measure: TOD street design features
mechanism: sprawl and sustainable mobility

ideas.test: Using a household travel survey (e.g., Seoul 2010), estimate SUR models of auto/transit trips with TOD design indices interacted with a sprawl/periphery indicator.
ideas.disconfirming: TOD design effects are equal or weaker in peripheral sprawling zones.

ideas.hypothesis: Greenfield mixed-use town centers generate trip rates closer to ITE single-use estimates than infill TODs do, so internal capture reductions are overestimated for suburban greenfield projects.

sources.role: method/finding: trip generation of greenfield mixed-use town square
finding: auto use of new housing near rail stations
mechanism: land use drives transportation outcomes
setting: suburban greenfield growth

ideas.test: Collect driveway counts at 5 greenfield mixed-use centers and 5 rail-adjacent TODs; compare observed trips to ITE and mixed-use method predictions.
ideas.disconfirming: Greenfield centers show the same or larger reductions from ITE estimates as TODs.

ideas.hypothesis: New Starts projects whose station areas had higher pre-existing mixed-use intensity received higher land-use ratings and achieved higher ridership relative to forecasts.

sources.role: mechanism: FTA uses land use in New Starts recommendations
setting: Exposition LRT TOD integration
mechanism: compact mixed-use linked to transit use
measure: auto use near rail stations

ideas.test: Assemble FTA land-use ratings and forecast vs actual ridership for 20-30 New Starts projects; compute station-area mixed-use entropy from land-use data and regress.
ideas.disconfirming: Mixed-use intensity is unrelated to land-use ratings or ridership performance.

ideas.hypothesis: FTA project evaluation favors rail over BRT in dense urban areas but BRT in lower-density areas, so density predicts mode selected among funded projects.

sources.role: mechanism: FTA encouragement of BRT and funding issues
mechanism: FTA land-use criteria
setting: dense urban LRT corridor

ideas.test: Logistic regression of mode (rail vs BRT) for FTA-funded capital projects 2000-2019 on corridor population/employment density.
ideas.disconfirming: Density does not predict mode choice among FTA-funded projects.

ideas.hypothesis: Federal transit funding per capita for capital projects is higher in denser urban areas, but the cost-effectiveness advantage is offset by more complex development integration costs.

sources.role: finding: complexities of TOD integration in dense settings
mechanism: funding constraints and lower-cost BRT

ideas.test: Merge FTA capital grant data with urbanized area density from census; regress funding per capita and cost per new rider on density.
ideas.disconfirming: Funding per capita does not increase with density, or cost per rider is unrelated to density.
